\chapter{Toward a Hermitian theory of \texorpdfstring{$\mathcal I$}{I}-goodness}
\label{chap:hermitian-igood}

The source book relates three descriptions of a singularity: approximation by analytic singularities, equality of a mass and a multiplier-ideal volume, and equality of two envelopes. The Hermitian problem is to determine when these descriptions remain equivalent. We construct the ideal envelope and compare it with the ordinary envelope without a mass hypothesis. The envelopes of dyadic analytic regularizations then give a precise monotone convergence criterion for their equality. This criterion will be distinguished from a topology on arbitrary singularity types and from a volume characterization.

\section{The source characterization}

For a closed big background on a compact K\"ahler manifold, and a potential $u$ of positive non-pluripolar mass, the source characterization theorem states the equivalence of
\[
 \begin{gathered}
 u\text{ lies in the }d_S\text{-closure of analytic singularities},\\
 \int_X\mathrm{MA}_\theta(u)
  =\int_X\mathrm{MA}_\theta(P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}),\\
 P_\theta[u]=P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}.
 \end{gathered}
\]
We recall this as an external input from \cite[Theorem~7.1.1]{SGPT}. Here $d_S$ is the source book's pseudometric on singularities, constructed from the K\"ahler geometry of potentials. We have not constructed such a metric for a general non-closed background.

The middle expression uses the source book's \emph{multiplier-ideal volume}. It is not either of the upper and lower volumes in \cref{def:singularity-volumes}. Those take a supremum or infimum over boundedly equivalent potentials, whereas the source expression first replaces $u$ by an envelope defined using multiplier ideals. We preserve this distinction in the notation below.

\section{An envelope defined by multiplier ideals}

Let $\theta$ be a smooth real background with $\PSH(X,\theta)\ne\varnothing$. Write $u\sim_{\mathcal I}v$ when
\[
 \mathcal I(\lambda u)=\mathcal I(\lambda v)
 \quad\text{for every }\lambda>0,
\]
using the weight $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda u}$ fixed in \cref{chap:framework}.

\begin{definition}\label{def:hermitian-i-envelope}
For $u\in\PSH(X,\theta)$ define
\[
 P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}
 :=\left(\sup\{v\in\PSH(X,\theta):v\leq0,
                   \ v\sim_{\mathcal I}u\}\right)^*.
\]
\end{definition}

The family is nonempty because $u-\sup_Xu$ belongs to it; bounded perturbations do not change multiplier ideals. It is bounded above by zero, so its regularized envelope is a genuine $\theta$-plurisubharmonic function. It depends only on the multiplier-ideal equivalence class of $u$. These statements require neither closedness nor a mass bound.

The definition alone does not prove that the supremum retains all the multiplier ideals of its competitors. We now supply that argument. The local inputs are the valuative characterization and strong openness recalled in the chapter on plurisubharmonic functions in \cite{SGPT}. We state the forms that we use, so their scope is explicit.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:local-i-inputs}
For germs of plurisubharmonic functions, the following facts hold.
\begin{enumerate}
\item Equality of multiplier ideals at every positive weight is equivalent to equality of the Lelong numbers of the pullbacks at every point on every local modification. Inclusion of the ideals at every positive weight is equivalent to the reverse inequalities for these Lelong numbers.
\item If $p_j$ is an increasing sequence of plurisubharmonic functions converging almost everywhere to a plurisubharmonic function $p$, then, for each point $x$ and each $\lambda>0$,
\[
 \mathcal I(\lambda p_j)_x=\mathcal I(\lambda p)_x
 \quad\text{for all sufficiently large }j.
\]
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}

In the first item one works over a coordinate neighborhood of the germ, allowing smaller neighborhoods as necessary. No assertion that every local modification extends to a modification of the compact manifold is needed. The local valuative criterion follows from the Boucksom--Favre--Jonsson theory and strong openness; the second item is the increasing-limit form of strong openness used in \cite{SGPT}. Smooth additions do not change multiplier ideals or Lelong numbers. Thus these inputs apply to quasi-plurisubharmonic functions after the local correction of \cref{prop:local-correction}.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:hermitian-i-calculus}
Suppose $u\sim_{\mathcal I}v$ and $u'\sim_{\mathcal I}v'$. Then
\[
 \max(u,u')\sim_{\mathcal I}\max(v,v'),\qquad
 u+u'\sim_{\mathcal I}v+v',\qquad
 a u\sim_{\mathcal I}a v\quad(a>0).
\]
These statements concern quasi-plurisubharmonic functions and require no background to be closed.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Fix a coordinate neighborhood and a local modification $\pi$. At every point $y$ above it, the elementary Lelong identities give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 \nu(\max(u,u')\circ\pi,y)
   &=\min\{\nu(u\circ\pi,y),\nu(u'\circ\pi,y)\},\\
 \nu((u+u')\circ\pi,y)
   &=\nu(u\circ\pi,y)+\nu(u'\circ\pi,y),\\
 \nu(a u\circ\pi,y)&=a\nu(u\circ\pi,y).
 \end{aligned}
\]
The corresponding expressions for $v,v'$ are equal by the first local input. Apply the converse direction of that input on each neighborhood. The Lelong identities are the usual local maximum, addition and scaling identities, unchanged by smooth corrections.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:hermitian-i-projection}
For every smooth real background $\theta$ and $u\in\PSH(X,\theta)$,
\[
 P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}\sim_{\mathcal I}u,\qquad
 P_\theta[P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}]_{\mathcal I}=P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}.
\]
The regularization in \cref{def:hermitian-i-envelope} does not change the pointwise supremum. Moreover,
\[
 \sup_X P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}=0.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $q=P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}$. By Choquet's lemma choose a sequence from the defining family whose regularized supremum is $q$. Replace it by successive finite maxima. By \cref{lem:hermitian-i-calculus}, the resulting sequence $v_j$ remains in the family, is increasing, and converges to $q$ almost everywhere.

Fix $x\in X$ and $\lambda>0$. On a coordinate ball about $x$, choose one smooth function $r$ such that every $v_j+r$ and $q+r$ is plurisubharmonic. This is possible because they all have the same smooth curvature lower bound $-\theta$. The second local input gives
\[
 \mathcal I(\lambda(q+r))_x
   =\mathcal I(\lambda(v_j+r))_x
   =\mathcal I(\lambda u)_x
\]
for large $j$; smooth additions give the second equality. Hence $q\sim_{\mathcal I}u$.

Since $q\leq0$, it now belongs to its own defining family. The pointwise supremum is at least $q$ and at most its regularization $q$, proving the assertion about regularization. The defining families for $P_\theta[q]_{\mathcal I}$ and $P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}$ coincide, which proves idempotence. Finally, if $\sup_Xq<0$, the function $q-\sup_Xq$ would be a larger competitor, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:p-below-i}
For every $u\in\PSH(X,\theta)$,
\[
 u-\sup_Xu\leq P_\theta[u]\leq P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}\leq V_\theta.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Only the middle inequality needs explanation. Let $h\leq0$ be $\theta$-plurisubharmonic with $h\preceq u$, and set
\[
 h'=\max(h,u-\sup_Xu).
\]
It is a normalized competitor below zero, dominates $h$, and differs from $u$ by a bounded amount. Hence $h'\sim_{\mathcal I}u$, so $h\leq P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}$. Take the regularized supremum over $h$. The last inequality holds because every competitor for $P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}$ is a competitor for $V_\theta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:ordinary-preserves-i}
For $u\in\PSH(X,\theta)$,
\[
 P_\theta[u]\sim_{\mathcal I}u,\qquad
 P_\theta[P_\theta[u]]_{\mathcal I}=P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I},\qquad
 P_\theta[P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}]=P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}.
\]
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The inequalities of \cref{prop:p-below-i} and monotonicity of local integrability give, for every $\lambda>0$,
\[
 \mathcal I(\lambda u)
 \subseteq\mathcal I(\lambda P_\theta[u])
 \subseteq\mathcal I(\lambda P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I})
 =\mathcal I(\lambda u).
\]
This proves the first assertion, and equality of the defining families proves the second. For $q=P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}$, the inequalities $q\leq P_\theta[q]\leq P_\theta[q]_{\mathcal I}=q$ prove the last assertion; the first inequality uses $q\leq0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:i-envelope-finite}
If $\theta$ is semipositive and big, then $P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}$ has finite extended Monge--Amp\`ere mass for every $u\in\PSH(X,\theta)$, without bounded mass on $X$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
The last identity in \cref{cor:ordinary-preserves-i} makes $P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}$ an ordinary envelope fixed point. Apply the fixed-point mass estimate in \cref{prop:fixed-point-finite}.
\end{proof}

The finiteness statement concerns the envelope. It does not imply finiteness for every function with the same multiplier ideals, as \cref{prop:goodness-infinite-mass} below demonstrates.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:i-envelope-operations}
Write $u\preceq_{\mathcal I}v$ if $\mathcal I(\lambda u)\subseteq\mathcal I(\lambda v)$ for every $\lambda>0$. Then
\[
 u\preceq_{\mathcal I}v\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
 P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}\leq P_\theta[v]_{\mathcal I}.
\]
For $a>0$ one has $P_{a\theta}[a u]_{\mathcal I}=aP_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}$. For potentials $u_i\in\PSH(X,\theta_i)$,
\[
 P_{\theta_1}[u_1]_{\mathcal I}+P_{\theta_2}[u_2]_{\mathcal I}
 \leq P_{\theta_1+\theta_2}[u_1+u_2]_{\mathcal I}.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $h$ is a competitor for $P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}$, the reverse Lelong inequalities in \cref{thm:local-i-inputs} show that $\max(h,v-\sup_Xv)$ is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $v$. It is below zero and dominates $h$. Taking the supremum proves order preservation. Scaling gives a bijection of the two defining families. For addition, the sum of the two envelopes is below zero, is $(\theta_1+\theta_2)$-plurisubharmonic, and is multiplier-ideal equivalent to $u_1+u_2$ by projection and \cref{lem:hermitian-i-calculus}. It is therefore an admissible competitor on the right.
\end{proof}

\Needspace{9\baselineskip}
\begin{proposition}\label{prop:i-envelope-gauge}
Let $\theta$ be a smooth real background, $u\in\PSH(X,\theta)$, and $f\in C^\infty(X,\mathbb R)$. Set $\theta'=\theta+\ddc f$, $u'=u-f$, $m=\min_Xf$ and $M=\max_Xf$. Then
\[
 P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}+m
 \leq P_{\theta'}[u']_{\mathcal I}+f
 \leq P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}+M.
\]
The identical inequalities hold for ordinary envelopes.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If $v$ is a competitor for $P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}$, then $v-f+m$ is $\theta'$-plurisubharmonic, below zero, and multiplier-ideal equivalent to $u'$. Therefore
$v\leq P_{\theta'}[u']_{\mathcal I}+f-m$.
Taking the envelope gives the first inequality. Conversely, a competitor $v'$ in the new background gives $v'+f-M$ in the old one, which proves the second inequality. For $P$, use the ordinary singularity order instead of multiplier-ideal equivalence in the same calculation.
\end{proof}

Thus changing the smooth representative gives envelopes whose associated currents have equivalent ordinary singularities in the same $\ddc$-class. Literal equality of the normalized potentials is not the gauge-invariant statement.

\section{Why the raw multiplier-ideal volume changes}

One might try to copy the source definition by putting
\[
 W_\theta(u)=\int_X\mathrm{MA}_\theta(P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}),
\]
whenever the integral is defined. In a non-closed background this quantity need not depend only on the current $\theta+\ddc u$.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:raw-i-volume-gauge-failure}
There are two smooth decompositions of the same positive current for which the corresponding values of $W$ are different.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Use the Hermitian form $\omega$ and smooth function $g=u_t$ from \cref{ex:torus-mass}, choosing $t\ne0$ sufficiently small. Both $\omega$ and $\omega'=\omega+\ddc g$ are Hermitian, and
\[
 \omega+\ddc0=\omega'+\ddc(-g).
\]
For a smooth potential in a Hermitian background, the multiplier ideals at all weights are trivial and zero is an admissible competitor for its multiplier-ideal envelope. That envelope is therefore zero. Consequently
\[
 W_\omega(0)=\int_X\omega^2,\qquad
 W_{\omega'}(-g)=\int_X(\omega+\ddc g)^2.
\]
The two integrals differ by the explicit formula \eqref{eq:torus-mass}.
\end{proof}

This obstruction persists on a complex manifold that is itself K\"ahler, and involves only smooth functions. The source proof of invariance uses closed-background mass invariance after identifying equivalent singularities; \cref{prop:i-envelope-gauge} supplies only the latter step.

There is a natural pair of replacements under bounded mass. For big $\theta$, define
\[
 \mathcal V^-_{\mathcal I,\theta}(u)
   =\underline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}),\qquad
 \mathcal V^+_{\mathcal I,\theta}(u)
   =\overline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}).
\]
They are finite and depend only on the multiplier-ideal class of $u$ in the fixed background. By \cref{prop:i-envelope-gauge} and gauge invariance of singularity volumes, they also depend only on the associated $\ddc$-class and the multiplier-ideal data, rather than on its smooth decomposition. Moreover, \cref{prop:p-below-i,thm:volume-monotonicity} give
\[
 \underline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(u)
 \leq\mathcal V^-_{\mathcal I,\theta}(u),\qquad
 \overline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(u)
 \leq\mathcal V^+_{\mathcal I,\theta}(u).
\]
These inequalities justify considering the two nonnegative gaps. They do not assert that either gap detects equality of envelopes without further hypotheses.

\section{Envelope equality outside bounded mass}

For the moment call
\begin{equation}\label{eq:background-goodness}
 P_\theta[u]=P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}
\end{equation}
\emph{envelope goodness in the fixed background}. This is a working definition. We have not proved independence under addition of an arbitrary positive background, nor equivalence with a closure of analytic singularities. Those are part of what makes the source notion more than a formal equality.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:goodness-infinite-mass}
If a Hermitian metric $\omega$ fails bounded mass, there exists $U\in\PSH(X,\omega)$ such that
\[
 P_\omega[U]=P_\omega[U]_{\mathcal I}=0,
 \qquad U\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\omega,0),
 \qquad \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega(U)(X)=+\infty.
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Take $U$ from \cref{prop:infinite-envelope-class}. Its ordinary envelope is zero and its multiplier ideals are trivial at every weight. Zero is consequently a competitor for $P_\omega[U]_{\mathcal I}$, and all such competitors are below zero. Thus $P_\omega[U]_{\mathcal I}=0$. The other properties have already been proved.
\end{proof}

For this potential, the raw envelope mass $W_\omega(U)=\int_X\omega^n$ is finite, while the mass of $U$ is infinite. Therefore the envelope equality in \eqref{eq:background-goodness} cannot imply the source raw mass-volume identity on the whole Hermitian potential space. The example supplies a concrete reason to impose a finite-mass regime or to replace the invariant before formulating an equivalence theorem.

\Needspace{8\baselineskip}
Positive divisorial currents supply another explicit regime for envelope equality. \Cref{cor:divisorial-current-ordinary-type} constructs a canonical ordinary type from a finite-mass divisorial current and a smooth residual form, and proves $P_\Omega[v]=P_\Omega[v]_{\mathcal I}\simeq v$ in every Hermitian background admitting that representative. The current may have infinitely many components. Exact curve-fibration trace types are examples; \cref{prop:exact-trace-infinite-representatives} still gives representatives of the same ideal class with different finiteness of Monge--Amp\`ere mass.

\section{A conditional characterization and the missing steps}

The following formal implication isolates part of the desired theory.

\Needspace{14\baselineskip}
\begin{proposition}\label{prop:conditional-i-characterization}
Assume bounded mass and a big background $\theta$. Let $u\in\PSH(X,\theta)$, and put $q=P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I}$. Suppose
\[
 \underline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(q)>0,
 \qquad u\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta,P_\theta[u]).
\]
Then the following are equivalent:
\[
 P_\theta[u]=P_\theta[u]_{\mathcal I},\qquad
 \overline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(u)
      =\mathcal V^+_{\mathcal I,\theta}(u).
\]
If they hold, the corresponding equality for the lower volume also holds.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
If the envelopes agree, the relative-class hypothesis puts $u$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta,q)$. The proof of \cref{thm:relative-equivalence} gives equality of both volumes with those of $q$.

Conversely, equality of the upper volumes, together with $u\preceq q$ from \cref{prop:p-below-i}, puts $u$ in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta,q)$. Positive lower volume and \cref{thm:relative-equivalence} imply membership in $\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta,q)$. By \cref{prop:relative-envelope-equality},
\[
 P_\theta[u]=P_\theta[q]=q,
\]
as required.
\end{proof}

The ordinary model identity $P_\theta[q]=q$ used in this proof is automatic by \cref{cor:ordinary-preserves-i}. The remaining displayed hypotheses are substantive. Under these hypotheses, \cref{cor:dyadic-goodness-criterion} also identifies equality of the upper volumes with convergence of the dyadic ordinary envelopes to $P_\theta[u]$. The remaining issue is to find intrinsic hypotheses ensuring the required positive lower volume and relative-class membership.

\begin{problem}\label{qu:hermitian-i-characterization}
For big non-closed backgrounds on manifolds with bounded mass, what is the weakest positive-volume assumption under which the hypotheses of \cref{prop:conditional-i-characterization} are automatic? Can that assumption be checked using only the ideal or divisorial data in the fixed background?
\end{problem}

This is a research question for the present manuscript, not a claim that every part is absent from the literature. In particular, the relative-envelope results in \cite{ALS26,XL26} already address parts of the modelization problem. The remaining comparison must preserve their precise hypotheses. A convergence defined through upper volumes should not be called a pseudometric until a triangle inequality has actually been proved.

\Needspace{10\baselineskip}
\begin{problem}\label{qu:i-good-no-bmp}
Construct a topology on ordinary singularity types in arbitrary Hermitian backgrounds for which the closure of analytic singularities is exactly the set satisfying $P_\omega[u]=P_\omega[u]_{\mathcal I}$. It should recover the dyadic-envelope criterion of \cref{cor:dyadic-goodness-criterion,cor:fixed-hermitian-analytic-density}, remain meaningful for infinite extended mass, and specify how convergence behaves under smooth changes of representative and background.
\end{problem}

The dyadic criterion identifies the limit of a specific ideal-controlled approximation; it does not yet define convergence for arbitrary families of ordinary singularity types. By \cref{cor:fixed-hermitian-analytic-density}, the elementary ideal metric makes analytic classes dense everywhere. The finite damped measures of \cref{chap:damped-measures} provide additional analytic data, but do not by themselves characterize multiplier ideals. Their capacity-continuity theorem also shows a limitation: on a normalized family, convergence in capacity already implies convergence of these damped measures. Merely appending damped weak convergence to capacity convergence adds no condition that could distinguish multiplier-ideal approximation. A convergence theory for arbitrary families must retain additional information about singularities, for example controlled ideal inclusions at each fixed weight. Constructing that theory remains open.

\chapter{Volumes under bounded mass}
\label{chap:mass-bound-volumes}

The upper and lower volumes in \cref{def:singularity-volumes} are defined as extended quantities in every smooth background. In this chapter $X$ has bounded mass and the backgrounds are big. These assumptions give finite invariants and comparison under changes of singularities. Positive lower volume will be imposed separately where it is used. The envelope constructions of \cref{chap:envelopes} remain available without these mass assumptions.

\section{Comparison of singularity volumes}

In a big background under bounded mass, these are \cite[Definition 3.1]{BGL25}, expressed in potentials, and
\[
 0\leq\underline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(u)
 \leq\int_X\mathrm{MA}_\theta(u)
 \leq\overline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(u)<+\infty.
\]
The uniform finiteness at the right is the content of the bounded mass estimates, not merely the finiteness of each individual integral.

Under bounded mass and bigness, if $\theta$ is also closed, both volumes equal $\int_X\mathrm{MA}_\theta(u)$; this uses invariance of the non-pluripolar mass under equivalent singularities, recalled in \cite[Example 3.2]{BGL25}. For a non-closed background this equality can fail even at $u=0$, as \cref{ex:torus-mass} shows.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:volume-monotonicity}
Suppose $\theta_1$ is big, $\theta_1\leq\theta_2$, and $u_i\in\PSH(X,\theta_i)$ satisfy $u_1\preceq u_2$. On a manifold with bounded mass,
\[
 \underline{\operatorname{vol}}_{\theta_1}(u_1)
 \leq\underline{\operatorname{vol}}_{\theta_2}(u_2),\qquad
 \overline{\operatorname{vol}}_{\theta_1}(u_1)
 \leq\overline{\operatorname{vol}}_{\theta_2}(u_2).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
We reconstruct \cite[Proposition 3.7]{BGL25} in the big regime. Shift $u_1$ so that $u_1\leq u_2$. Choose $v_2\simeq u_2$ in $\PSH(X,\theta_2)$ and set
\[
 p_t=P_{\theta_1}(u_1+t,v_2).
\]
For $t>0$, a sufficiently low constant translate of $u_1$ is a competitor; also $p_t\leq u_1+t$. Thus $p_t\simeq u_1$. The contact theorem, applied in each background on the corresponding contact part, and positivity of the mixed products give
\[
 \mathrm{MA}_{\theta_1}(p_t)
 \leq\mathbf1_{\{u_1\leq v_2-t\}}\mathrm{MA}_{\theta_1}(u_1)
      +\mathrm{MA}_{\theta_2}(v_2).
\]
Indeed $p_t$ is also $\theta_2$-plurisubharmonic and is below $v_2$, so the contact inequality in that background applies. The first measure on the right has mass tending to zero: its indicators tend to zero off the pole sets, and the measure is finite and non-pluripolar. Integrate, let $t\to+\infty$, and then take the infimum over $v_2$.

For the upper volume, choose any $v_1\simeq u_1$ in $\PSH(X,\theta_1)$ and put $w_t=\max(v_1,u_2-t)$. It is $\theta_2$-plurisubharmonic and $w_t\simeq u_2$. On $D_t=\{v_1>u_2-t\}$, locality and mixed-product positivity imply
\[
 \mathbf1_{D_t}\mathrm{MA}_{\theta_1}(v_1)
 \leq\mathbf1_{D_t}\mathrm{MA}_{\theta_2}(w_t).
\]
The sets $D_t$ exhaust the complement of a pluripolar set. Hence integration and passage to the limit give
$\int_X\mathrm{MA}_{\theta_1}(v_1)\leq
\overline{\operatorname{vol}}_{\theta_2}(u_2)$.
Take the supremum over $v_1$. This proof does not require $v_1$ to be bounded.
\end{proof}

The theorem orders the backgrounds and the potentials separately. These hypotheses should not be confused with ordering the two currents $\theta_i+\ddc u_i$.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:volume-addition}
Assume bounded mass. Let $\theta$ be big, $u\in\PSH(X,\theta)$, and $v\in\PSH(X,\eta)$ for a smooth real form $\eta$. Then, for either the lower or the upper volume,
\[
 \operatorname{vol}_\theta(u)
 \leq\operatorname{vol}_{\theta+\eta}(u+v).
\]
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
The form $\theta+\eta$ is big, by adding the positive current $\eta+\ddc v$ to a strictly positive current in the class of $\theta$. For the upper volume, add $v$ to each competitor for $u$. Positivity of mixed products shows that the resulting mass is at least the original mass.

For the lower volume, choose $w\simeq u+v$ in $\PSH(X,\theta+\eta)$, and let $p=P_\theta(w-v)$. Since $w-v=u+O(1)$ outside the pole sets, the envelope is genuine and $p\simeq u$. The contact theorem says that its measure is carried by $D=\{p+v=w\}$. Furthermore $p+v\leq w$ everywhere, since this inequality holds off a pluripolar set between canonical quasi-plurisubharmonic functions. Thus
\[
 \mathrm{MA}_\theta(p)
 \leq\mathbf1_D\mathrm{MA}_{\theta+\eta}(p+v)
 \leq\mathbf1_D\mathrm{MA}_{\theta+\eta}(w).
\]
Integrating and taking the infimum over $w$ proves the assertion. This is the envelope proof of \cite[Proposition 2.5]{XL26}.
\end{proof}

\section{Relative full mass}

\begin{definition}\label{def:relative-volume-class}
Define
\[
 \mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta,\varphi)
 =\{u\in\PSH(X,\theta):u\preceq\varphi,
 \ \overline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(u)
   =\overline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(\varphi)\}.
\]
\end{definition}

This is \cite[Definition 3.2]{XL26}. The next theorem compares it with the envelope class of \cref{def:relative-envelope-class}.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:relative-equivalence}
Suppose $X$ has bounded mass, $\theta$ is big, and
$\underline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(\varphi)>0$. Then
\[
 \mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta,\varphi)
 =\mathcal E_{\mathrm{vol}}(X,\theta,\varphi).
\]
Every member also satisfies
$\underline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(u)
=\underline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(\varphi)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First assume the envelope condition. For each $a\in(0,1)$ there is $h\in\PSH(X,\theta)$ such that $a\varphi+(1-a)h\leq u$. By \cref{thm:volume-monotonicity,prop:volume-addition} and homogeneity, for either volume,
\[
 a^n\operatorname{vol}_\theta(\varphi)
 \leq\operatorname{vol}_\theta(a\varphi+(1-a)h)
 \leq\operatorname{vol}_\theta(u)
 \leq\operatorname{vol}_\theta(\varphi).
\]
Let $a\to1$. This proves equality of both volumes in this direction, even without positive lower volume.

Conversely, suppose equality of the upper volumes, and fix $b>1$. Shift the potentials so that $u\leq\varphi\leq0$, and put
\[
 u_j=\max(u,\varphi-j),\qquad q_j=Q_b(u_j,\varphi).
\]
Each $q_j$ is genuine and equivalent to $\varphi$: the lower competitor $\varphi-bj$ and the defining inequality give
$\varphi-bj\leq q_j\leq\varphi$.
The sequence decreases. If its limit were $-\infty$, the compactness and Hartogs lemma for normalized quasi-plurisubharmonic functions would give $\sup_Xq_j\to-\infty$.

Set $C_j=\{b^{-1}q_j+(1-b^{-1})\varphi=u_j\}$. The contact theorem and positivity of mixed products give
\[
 \mathrm{MA}_\theta(q_j)
 \leq b^n\mathbf1_{C_j}\mathrm{MA}_\theta(u_j).
\]
On $C_j\cap\{q_j\leq-bk\}$, the inequality $\varphi\leq0$ implies $u_j\leq-k$, hence $u\leq-k$. For $j>k$, locality on $\{u>-k\}\subset\{u>\varphi-j\}$ therefore yields
\[
 \begin{split}
 \int_{\{q_j\leq-bk\}}\mathrm{MA}_\theta(q_j)
 &\leq b^n\int_{\{u\leq-k\}}\mathrm{MA}_\theta(u_j)\\
 &\leq b^n\left(
 \overline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(\varphi)
 -\int_{\{u>-k\}}\mathrm{MA}_\theta(u)\right).
 \end{split}
\]
If $\sup_Xq_j\to-\infty$, the domain on the left is all of $X$ for large $j$. It follows, on letting $k\to+\infty$, that
\[
 \underline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(\varphi)
 \leq b^n\left(
 \overline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(\varphi)
 -\int_X\mathrm{MA}_\theta(u)\right).
\]
The same collapse would hold with any $u'\simeq u$ in place of $u$: a competitor for either target gives one for the other by a constant translation. Repeating the argument and taking the supremum of $\int_X\mathrm{MA}_\theta(u')$ gives
\[
 \underline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(\varphi)
 \leq b^n\left(
 \overline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(\varphi)
 -\overline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(u)\right)=0,
\]
a contradiction. Thus $Q_b(u,\varphi)$ is genuine for every $b$. The argument is the full-volume case of \cite[Lemma 3.1]{XL26}; the proof uses bounded mass and the displayed positive lower volume, without a separate global positive volume hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\section{Model references with positive lower volume}

For a big, possibly non-semipositive form under bounded mass, Li uses
\begin{equation}\label{eq:li-model-condition}
 P_\theta[\varphi]=\varphi,\qquad
 \underline{\operatorname{vol}}_\theta(\varphi)>0.
\end{equation}

In the latter assertion $\theta$ is semipositive and big, and the reference is an ordinary envelope fixed point. The smaller-background condition \eqref{eq:als-model-condition} does not itself assert a uniform positive lower mass. Its no-mass-bound consequences were proved in \cref{sec:relative-envelope-room}.

\chapter{Equations with prescribed singularities}
\label{chap:prescribed-equations}

There are two ways to prescribe singularities in a Monge--Amp\`ere equation. One can require the solution to differ from a reference potential by a bounded function. Alternatively, one can require it to belong to a relative full mass class; the solution may then be strictly more singular than the reference. The distinction is already present in the closed theory. In the Hermitian theory it interacts with the choice of upper and lower volume, and with the positivity assumptions needed for domination.

We first solve $L^p$ equations in semipositive big backgrounds and develop the comparison and compactness arguments used later. These also describe what the positive-exponent approximation selects in the nonuniqueness example. For arbitrary smooth big backgrounds, \cref{sec:big-minimal-comparison,sec:big-minimal-existence} use a strict singular barrier, resolution and the Gauduchon trace to solve both equations in the minimal ordinary singularity type, without either metric volume property. The next step prescribes a general ordinary type in a semipositive background.

In a Hermitian background, \cref{sec:lower-mass-solvability} explains why positive lower mass is necessary for solvability for every finite non-pluripolar measure. The general-measure existence theorems under uniform mass hypotheses are collected in \cref{chap:relative-finite-measures,chap:bounded-mass-equations}. The present chapter treats the admissibility and approximation of individual right-hand sides without imposing either metric mass property.

For an individual $L^1$ density, \cref{sec:individual-density-subsolutions,sec:integrable-gauduchon-tests,sec:individual-density-stability} replace this uniform hypothesis by an exact subsolution threshold and its Gauduchon formula. The final sections construct the greatest exponential solution at a positive threshold and separate convergence of the scalar, the right-hand-side measure and the normalized potential. Throughout, uniqueness of the scalar is distinguished from uniqueness of the potential.

\]
has a uniform $L^q$ bound. More explicitly, choose $q<p$ first, apply H\"older with exponents $p/q$ and $p/(p-q)$, and then choose $\gamma$ small enough to control the exponential factor by Cauchy--Schwarz and the two exponential integrability estimates.

Apply \cref{thm:big-bounded-normalized} in background $(1-\varepsilon)\theta$ to the density $1+g$. We obtain a bounded $v$, with $\sup_Xv=0$, and $c>0$ such that
\[
 ((1-\varepsilon)\theta+\ddc v)^n=c(1+g)\,\mathrm{d}V.
\]
Both $\|v\|_\infty$ and $c^{-1}$ are uniformly bounded. The added constant one ensures a uniform positive root integral, even if no lower bound for the integral of $f$ was specified.

Put $h=\varphi_\varepsilon+v\leq\varphi$ and define
\[
 \chi(t)=\frac1{1-t}\quad(t\leq0),\qquad
 \psi=\varphi+\chi(h-\varphi).
\]
Then $0\leq\chi\leq1$, $0<\chi'\leq1$, and $\chi''>0$. The formula is interpreted off the pole sets and then by the canonical representative. We justify it as follows. The function
$G(x,y)=x+\chi(y-x)$ on $y\leq x$ is convex and nondecreasing in each variable: its first derivatives are $1-\chi'$ and $\chi'$, and its Hessian is
\[
 \chi''\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}\geq0.
\]
For bounded ordered potentials the local chain rule therefore gives
\[
 \theta+\ddc G(\varphi,h)
 \geq(1-\chi'(h-\varphi))\theta_\varphi
       +\chi'(h-\varphi)\theta_h\geq0.
\]
This bounded chain rule follows by local convolution after a common smooth correction; $G(x+r,y+r)=r+G(x,y)$ preserves that correction, and positivity follows by the same constant-form freezing used for bounded products. For unbounded potentials apply the bounded assertion to
$\varphi_k=\max(\varphi,-k)$ and $h_k=\max(h,-k)\leq\varphi_k$. Monotonicity of $G$ makes $G(\varphi_k,h_k)$ decrease. Its limit is $\theta$-plurisubharmonic and lies between $\varphi$ and $\varphi+1$, so it is genuine and equals $\psi$ as defined above. Locality on common finite levels and bounded product positivity give
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(\psi)
 \geq(\varphi-h+1)^{-2n}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(h)
 \geq c(\varphi-h+1)^{-2n}\mathrm{e}^{-\gamma\varphi_\varepsilon}
             \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma u}f\,\mathrm{d}V.
\]
Pole sets have zero smooth volume, so the last inequality extends by exhaustion to all Borel sets.

Write $T=-\varphi_\varepsilon\geq0$. If $C\geq1+\|v\|_\infty$, then
$\varphi-h+1\leq T+C$. Since
\[
 A:=\inf_{T\geq0}\frac{\mathrm{e}^{\gamma T}}{(T+C)^{2n}}>0,
\]
we obtain, with a uniform $d>0$,
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(\psi)
 \geq d \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma u}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(u).
\]
Choose $K=2+\gamma^{-1}|\log d|$. On $\{u<\psi-K\}$ we have $u<1-K$, hence
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(u)
 \leq d^{-1}\mathrm{e}^{\gamma(1-K)}
            \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(\psi-K)
 \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\gamma}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(\psi-K).
\]
The two potentials have the same ordinary singularity type. Moreover $P_{\varepsilon\theta}(u)$ is genuine, since $u\geq\varphi-C_u$ for some constant $C_u$. Singular strict domination yields $u\geq\psi-K\geq\varphi-K$. All constants used to choose $K$ are uniform in the asserted family. The possibly nonuniform $C_u$ is used only to provide a genuine envelope, not in any estimate.
\end{proof}

The estimate controls $u-\varphi$, rather than $u$ itself. The smaller-background condition supplies $\varphi_\varepsilon$ and enables the final domination argument; the bounded auxiliary equation is now supplied by the preceding sections.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:relative-lp-supersolution}
For nonzero $0\leq f\in L^p(\mathrm{d}V)$ and $\lambda>0$, there exists $w\simeq\varphi$ such that
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(w)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda w}f\,\mathrm{d}V.
\]
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Let $v$ be the bounded solution of \cref{thm:big-bounded-exponential}, and write $M=\sup_Xv$, $a=v-M\leq0$. The rooftop $p=P_\theta(a,\varphi)$ satisfies
$\varphi-\|a\|_\infty\leq p\leq\varphi$, so $p\simeq\varphi$. By the rooftop inequality,
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(p)
 \leq\mathbf1_{\{p=a\leq\varphi\}}\mathrm{MA}_\theta(a)
   +\mathbf1_{\{p=\varphi<a\}}\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(\varphi).
\]
The second term vanishes: \cref{prop:fixed-point-finite} carries the measure of $\varphi$ on $\{\varphi=0\}$, while $\varphi<a\leq0$ excludes that set. On the first contact set, $a=p$ and
$\mathrm{MA}_\theta(a)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda(a+M)}f\,\mathrm{d}V$. Thus
$\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(p)\leq \mathrm{e}^{\lambda(p+M)}f\,\mathrm{d}V$. Take $w=p+M$. This is the argument of \cite[Lemma 5.6]{ALS26}.
\end{proof}

\section{The zero-exponent limit and its topology}
\label{sec:zero-exponent-topology}

The uniform limit $\lambda u_\lambda\to\log c$ proved for continuous bounded potentials in \cref{chap:weak-equations} cannot be transferred unchanged to an unbounded prescribed singularity type.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:singular-no-uniform-limit}
Suppose $\varphi$ is unbounded below and $u_\lambda\simeq\varphi$ for every $\lambda>0$. Then $\lambda u_\lambda$ cannot converge uniformly on $X$ to a finite constant as $\lambda\downarrow0$. Its distance to any finite constant is also infinite in $L^\infty(\mathrm{d}V)$ for each fixed $\lambda>0$.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Bounded equivalence preserves unboundedness below. Every nonempty strict sublevel set of the upper semicontinuous function $u_\lambda$ is open and has positive smooth volume. Thus $u_\lambda$ is essentially unbounded below, as is $\lambda u_\lambda$. The stated conclusions follow.
\end{proof}

A fixed finite non-pluripolar measure is uniformly controlled by capacity.

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:npp-uniform-capacity}
Let $\mu$ be a finite non-pluripolar Borel measure on $X$. Then
\[
 \lim_{\delta\downarrow0}\sup\{\mu(E):E\text{ Borel},\
                      \operatorname{Cap}_\omega(E)\leq\delta\}=0.
\]
Consequently, capacity convergence implies convergence in $\mu$-measure.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
If the first assertion failed, there would be $\epsilon>0$ and Borel sets $E_j$ with capacity at most $2^{-j}$ and $\mu(E_j)\geq\epsilon$. Countable subadditivity of capacity gives
\[
 \operatorname{Cap}_\omega\left(\limsup_j E_j\right)=0.
\]
The limsup is therefore pluripolar and has zero $\mu$-measure. On the other hand, finiteness of $\mu$ and continuity from above applied to $\bigcup_{j\geq k}E_j$ show that the limsup has measure at least $\epsilon$, a contradiction. Apply the first assertion to the sets on which the difference of two converging potentials exceeds a fixed positive number to get the consequence.
\end{proof}

For solutions of $\mathrm{MA}_\theta(u_\lambda)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_\lambda}\mu$, write
\[
 v_\lambda=u_\lambda-\sup_Xu_\lambda,\qquad
 c_\lambda=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda\sup_Xu_\lambda}.
\]
There are three separate limit questions: whether $c_\lambda$ has a finite limit, whether the measures $c_\lambda\mathrm{e}^{\lambda v_\lambda}\mu$ converge, and whether a limit of $v_\lambda$ solves the resulting equation. The next lemma passes from the first question to the second for every fixed finite non-pluripolar measure. The third requires a continuity theorem for the Monge--Amp\`ere operator. For $L^p$ densities, the measure estimate is quantitative.

\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
\begin{lemma}\label{lem:normalized-exponential-lp}\label{lem:normalized-exponential-npp}
Let $v_j\in\PSH(X,\theta)$ satisfy $\sup_Xv_j=0$, and let $\lambda_j>0$ decrease to zero. For every finite non-pluripolar measure $\mu$,
\[
 \int_X\left|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_jv_j}-1\right|\,\mathrm{d}\mu\longrightarrow0.
\]
If $f\in L^p(\mathrm{d}V)$ for some $p>1$, then more precisely
\[
 \int_X\left|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_jv_j}-1\right|\,|f|\,\mathrm{d}V
 \leq C_p\lambda_j\|f\|_{L^p(\mathrm{d}V)}.
\]
The constant depends on the fixed background, $p$ and $\mathrm{d}V$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
Choose a Hermitian form $\Omega\geq\theta$. By \cref{lem:global-capacity-estimates}, for every $T>1$,
\[
 \operatorname{Cap}_\Omega(\{v_j<-T\})\leq C/T
\]
uniformly in $j$. Since $v_j\leq0$, splitting at this sublevel gives
\[
 \int_X(1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_jv_j})\,\mathrm{d}\mu
 \leq\lambda_jT\mu(X)+\mu(\{v_j<-T\}).
\]
The preceding lemma makes the second term uniformly small when $T$ is large. For this fixed $T$, the first term tends to zero as $j\to\infty$. This proves the general assertion. The value of the exponential is zero at a pole; pole sets have zero $\mu$-measure.

For the quantitative assertion, \cref{lem:uniform-exponential}, applied in background $\Omega$, gives a uniform $L^q$ bound for $-v_j$, where $q=p/(p-1)$. H\"older's inequality and
\[
 0\leq1-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_jv_j}\leq\lambda_j|v_j|
\]
give the claimed estimate for every $j$.
\end{proof}

Consequently, if $u_j$ solve $\mathrm{MA}_\theta(u_j)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_ju_j}f\,\mathrm{d}V$, put
\[
 v_j=u_j-\sup_Xu_j,\qquad c_j=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_j\sup_Xu_j}.
\]
If $c_j\to c<+\infty$, then the right-hand sides
$c_j\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_jv_j}f\,\mathrm{d}V$ converge in total variation to $cf\,\mathrm{d}V$. This conclusion follows from the lemma alone. To conclude that an $L^1$ limit of $v_j$ solves the limiting equation still requires continuity of the Monge--Amp\`ere operator and preservation of the relative class.

Here is one precise continuity input that supplies this step in a common regime.

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:relative-dominated-continuity}
Assume the hypotheses on $\theta,\varphi$ of \cref{thm:als-general-measure}. Suppose $u_j\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta,\varphi)$, $u_j\to u\in\PSH(X,\theta)$ in $L^1(X)$, and
\[
 \mathrm{MA}_\theta(u_j)\leq\nu
\]
for one finite non-pluripolar measure $\nu$. Then $u\in\mathcal E_{\mathrm{env}}(X,\theta,\varphi)$, the convergence holds in capacity, and
$\mathrm{MA}_\theta(u_j)\rightharpoonup\mathrm{MA}_\theta(u)$.
\end{theorem}

This is the fixed-measure case of \cite[Lemma 4.2 and Theorem 4.1, condition (2)]{ALS26}. A complete reconstruction is given in \cref{thm:relative-fixed-measure-continuity}. Its proof first constructs a common rooftop envelope after extraction, establishes finite mass of the limiting lower roofs, and then applies domination. Mere $L^1$ convergence, even for uniformly bounded potentials, is insufficient for the Monge--Amp\`ere passage to the limit. The common dominating measure and the positive lower mass assumption are the substantive hypotheses here.

\section[Exponential approximation without bounded mass]{Closing an exponential approximation without bounded mass}
\label{sec:exponential-closedness}

The estimates in \cref{chap:damped-measures} give a passage to the limit that requires neither bounded mass nor a positive lower volume. Its hypothesis is convergence in capacity. Establishing that convergence in an existence argument remains a separate task.

\Needspace{15\baselineskip}
\begin{theorem}\label{thm:exponential-closedness}
Fix a Hermitian metric on $X$, let $\theta$ be any smooth real $(1,1)$-form, and let $\mu$ be a finite non-pluripolar measure. Suppose $f_j\geq0$, $f_j\to f$ in $L^1(\mu)$, and $\lambda_j>0$ with $\lambda_j\to\lambda>0$. Let $u_j,u\in\PSH(X,\theta)$ be nonpositive, suppose $u_j\to u$ in capacity, and assume
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(u_j)
     =\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_j u_j}f_j\,\mu.
\]
Then $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(u)$ is finite and
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(u)=\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f\,\mu.
\]
The measures on the left converge weakly; the right-hand sides converge in total variation.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Discard finitely many indices so that $\lambda_j\geq\lambda/2$. Their masses are at most $\|f_j\|_{L^1(\mu)}$, hence uniformly bounded. On a deep sublevel,
\[
 \mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\theta(u_j)(\{u_j<-T\})
 \leq \mathrm{e}^{-\lambda T/2}\|f_j\|_{L^1(\mu)}.
\]
The tail criterion \cref{thm:undamped-tail-continuity}, in its general-background form \cref{thm:general-background-damping}, shows that the limiting Monge--Amp\`ere measure is finite and that the left-hand sides converge weakly to it.

It remains to identify this weak limit. By \cref{lem:npp-uniform-capacity}, $u_j\to u$ in $\mu$-measure. The functions $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u_j}$ are bounded by one and converge in $\mu$-measure to $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$. The change of exponent is uniform for nonpositive arguments, because the mean-value theorem gives
\[
 \sup_{t\leq0}|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_jt}-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}|
 \leq |\lambda_j-\lambda|
       \sup_{s\geq0}s \mathrm{e}^{-(\lambda/2)s}\longrightarrow0.
\]
Thus $\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_j u_j}\to \mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}$ in $\mu$-measure and, by absolute continuity, in $f\mu$-measure as well. Boundedness by one and finiteness of $f\mu$ give convergence in $L^1(f\mu)$. Therefore
\[
 \begin{split}
 \int_X|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_j u_j}f_j-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}f|\,\mathrm{d}\mu
 &\leq\|f_j-f\|_{L^1(\mu)}\\
 &\quad+\int_X|\mathrm{e}^{\lambda_j u_j}-\mathrm{e}^{\lambda u}|f\,\mathrm{d}\mu
 \longrightarrow0.
 \end{split}
\]
This proves total-variation convergence and identifies the equation for $u$.
\end{proof}

Normalizing constants can be absorbed into $f_j$ whenever the resulting densities converge in $L^1(\mu)$. The theorem does not assert that an arbitrary $L^1$-convergent sequence converges in capacity or stays in a prescribed envelope class.

This argument also pinpoints the difficulty as $\lambda_j\downarrow0$: the tail bound $\mathrm{e}^{-\lambda_jT}\|f_j\|_1$ no longer tends to zero uniformly in $j$ as $T\to\infty$. A zero-exponent approximation needs another source of uniform tail control, such as the integrability condition in \cref{cor:integrability-continuity}. Global bounded mass would not by itself supply that missing tail estimate.

\Needspace{19\baselineskip}
\section{Consequences for the singularity program}

Ordinary singularity volumes are defined by optimizing mass within a bounded-equivalence class. They are therefore invariants of that class and may be infinite; their finiteness and comparison properties retain the hypotheses of \cref{chap:envelopes}. Multiplier-ideal equivalence is coarser. The $\mathcal I$-goodness problem asks which envelope and volume identities survive under this coarser relation.

The equation proofs separate three ingredients: relative envelopes, finite damped measures and continuity of the undamped operator. The first two are available without bounded mass. The third requires estimates for the actual approximating sequence, as in \cref{thm:exponential-closedness}.

Gauduchon metrics give an invariant linear trace and the adjoint measure controlling the smooth scalar. In \cref{chap:normalization}, logarithmic variation of the density gives supporting probabilities for prescribed-type equations. Their construction does not identify them with a linearized adjoint at a singular solution; that identification requires additional regularity.
